In the weeks that followed, we got pushback from members of Congress, Democratic donors, and pro-Israel media outlets and personalities. Their complaints were similar. Why hadn’t Obama traveled to Israel in addition to Egypt? Why hadn’t he referred to Israel as the historic homeland of the Jewish people? Why hadn’t he recognized Israel as a Jewish state? Over time those demands made their way into Obama’s speeches as we succumbed to the drumbeat around us.

This pattern repeated itself over eight years. For the most pro-Israel elements of the organized American Jewish community, the guiding principle has been that there should be “no daylight” between the United States and Israel. Indeed, in 2009, when Obama suggested in a meeting with community leaders that he’d have more credibility as a defender of Israel if he occasionally differed with its government, it led to attacks that persisted for years. However, the burden of ensuring US and Israeli unity was entirely on Obama: unless he aligned his public positions with those of Netanyahu, a right-winger who presided over a military occupation of Palestinian land in what I consider an apartheid system, he would pay a political price.

When Obama did break with Netanyahu—in calling for the borders of a future Palestinian state to be based on the 1967 lines with agreed-on land swaps, or in barring photographers from a meeting between the two of them—days of controversy and hyperbolic media coverage followed. Aggravated Democratic members of Congress and donors lit up the White House phone lines. Meanwhile, like clockwork, new pro-Israel legislation—providing weapons or sanctioning Iran—was introduced each year around the time of AIPAC’s policy conference in Washington and passed with overwhelming bipartisan support.

To his credit, Obama defied the wishes of an Israeli prime minister more substantially than any other president this century. Just to have the space to negotiate his nuclear deal with Iran, Obama told Democrats in the House and the Senate that he would veto their AIPAC-backed Iran sanctions bills. The result was the unprecedented sight, in 2015, of a Republican Speaker of the House inviting the prime minister of a foreign country to deliver a speech to Congress in which he lambasted American foreign policy, demanded a confrontation with Iran, and won bipartisan standing ovations for it.

When the 2015 nuclear deal was completed, pro-Israel groups spent tens of millions of dollars trying to kill it. I led a two-month effort from the Obama White House in which we relentlessly briefed and cajoled Democratic senators just to ensure we had forty votes to sustain it in the Senate. Ask yourself: Why is it so much easier to take the United States to war than to forge a diplomatic agreement to avoid one?

The enormous political capital spent in the process made it feel impossible to buck other pro-Israel priorities. After the bruising fight over the Iran deal, the Obama administration (shamefully, in retrospect) gave Netanyahu a ten-year, $38 billion memorandum of understanding for military assistance despite his intransigence on Iran and Palestine; the House of Representatives voted 405–4 to endorse it. The price of violating the no daylight rule, as with the fallout from the Cairo speech, was giving Israel other things that it wanted.

This cycle of pressure and expected accommodation inevitably shapes the behavior of the people carrying out foreign policy, who like to claim that they operate independently of politics. In private, my colleagues were often withering about Israel’s conduct. But voicing such thoughts in public was understood to be career suicide. Consider just one example. Sarah Margon, Biden’s nominee to be the State Department’s senior official responsible for democracy and human rights, was unable to achieve Senate confirmation because she once tweeted in support of Airbnb’s short-lived boycott of West Bank settlements.

Or consider me. During the Obama administration, I was known in Washington to be a critic of Israel’s policies and a pugnacious defender of the Iran deal. Yet you can find footage of me online reiterating Israel’s right to defend itself in Gaza, trumpeting the unprecedented security assistance that we provided, and reciting talking points about a two-state solution while the Israeli government was making that an impossibility. At the time it felt anodyne; in retrospect it doesn’t.

Still, by the end of the Obama administration, the pro-Israel media was attacking me relentlessly and prominent donors were occasionally chewing me out. In 2018 I learned through press reports that a group of former Mossad agents known as Black Cube was digging up dirt on me. Operatives had even contacted my wife under the false pretense of being a movie production company: the aptly named “Shell Productions.” None of this was subtle. Indeed it was so heavy handed that it almost seemed as if Black Cube wanted these efforts to become public. Perhaps that was the point of the vitriol directed at me: to show other people working in US national security what they could expect if they strayed from the no daylight approach.

Among the American national security and political class, the belief that you can’t challenge Israel has become so entrenched that officials experience support for Israel not as a choice but as incontestable. It calls to mind Italo Calvino’s observation about America: “Here we are in a totalitarian structure of a medieval kind, based on the fact that no alternative exists nor even any awareness of the possibility of an alternative.”

Ahmed describes a photo that Biden once inscribed to Netanyahu with the words “Bibi, I don’t agree with a damn thing you say but I love you.” I heard Biden use that same formulation several times when I worked with him in the Obama White House. I always wondered: But why do you love him?

Biden was typical of US officials in his support for Israel but atypical in the ardor of that support. During his vice-presidency, he was at times uncomfortable with Obama’s willingness to publicly break with Netanyahu. He made it clear during his 2020 campaign that he would take a different approach. He rejected a progressive demand to simply refer to Israel’s “occupation” of the West Bank and Gaza in the Democratic Party platform. In response to calls to make assistance to Israel conditional on its actions, Antony Blinken—the future secretary of state—told the Democratic Majority for Israel that Biden “would not tie military assistance to Israel to any political decisions that it makes, period, full stop.”

This approach carried over into Biden’s presidency. Ahmed usefully reviews the administration’s record prior to October 7, 2023. Biden embraced the Abraham Accords—a deal brokered by Jared Kushner between the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, and Israel that made Palestinians irrelevant to the pursuit of “peace” between Israel and the Arab world—as a centerpiece of his Middle East policy. He broke a campaign promise to reenter Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, from which Donald Trump had withdrawn, and demanded a “longer and stronger” agreement in language that echoed the deal’s pro-Israel critics. He continued punitive policies initiated by the first Trump administration, failing to restore Palestinian representation in Washington and to reopen a US consulate in East Jerusalem. “Biden,” Ahmed writes, “notably became the first president since Richard Nixon to not even propose a road map for Israeli-Palestinian peace.”

Instead Biden and his team focused on bringing Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords, dangling before Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman the prospect of a mutual defense pact and a civil nuclear program. Such an agreement would have upended decades of Saudi policy, which based recognition of Israel on the creation of a Palestinian state. This fact was not lost on either bin Salman or the Palestinians. In fact, according to The Times of Israel, records obtained from private Hamas meetings stated plainly that one of the motives behind the October 7 attacks was “to thwart the Saudi kingdom’s process of normalization.”

There is no justification for the terror and brutality unleashed by Hamas on that horrific day. But in the Biden administration’s policies before October 7, we see the seeds of its support for the terror and brutality that Israel unleashed on the people of Gaza: No conditions on aid to Israel. No public breaks with Netanyahu. Little regard for the plight of the Palestinians.

Ahmed’s account of the administration’s initial decisions after October 7 is both chilling and familiar. Israel’s intentions were clear from the start. Netanyahu vowed to make Gaza a “deserted island.” Yoav Gallant, Israel’s defense minister, declared that he had “ordered a complete siege on the Gaza Strip. There will be no electricity, no food, no fuel.” Rather than a military campaign against Hamas, Israel’s leaders were pledging to inflict collective punishment on two million men, women, and children: an open statement of intent to commit a war crime.

In response, the Biden administration fast-tracked shipments of weapons that Israel needed to carry out its assault. The White House clearly thought that this was both the right policy and good politics for Biden’s reelection campaign, Ahmed writes: “Many of the voices the administration saw as most relevant vindicated Biden’s posture, like pro-Israel groups and donors with influence in policy circles and, crucially, the election.” Ahmed painfully records the administration’s disregard for Arab American citizens trapped in Gaza as it focused relentlessly on recovering Jewish American citizens held hostage by Hamas.

Biden underscored this unequal valuation of human life at a press conference on October 25, 2023. “I have no notion that the Palestinians are telling the truth about how many people are killed,” he declared, even though his administration was using the Gaza Health Ministry’s numbers in its casualty assessments.

Most of Crossing the Red Line tells the story of how officials sustained their unconditional support for Israel until the bitter end of the Biden administration. “The Gaza policy circle was small and insular,” Ahmed writes, a description that feels familiar. In the Obama years, matters of sensitivity or presidential priority were dealt with not in a cabinet-level or interagency meeting but rather by a “small group” led by the national security adviser. This allowed the president to maintain tight control over a policy; intentionally or not, it also limited the scope of dissenting voices.

The top of Biden’s policy circle was, in Ahmed’s reporting, National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan, the White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, and Secretary of State Antony Blinken. Ahmed had little access to these players—although McGurk, whom Ahmed singles out for the breadth of his bureaucratic maneuvering on behalf of Israel, enters the story when, at an event, he directly confronts Ahmed over his coverage. To compensate, Ahmed often relied on midlevel officials from the National Security Council, the State Department, and USAID. This gives the reader the strangely riveting perspective of aides who experienced the contorted rationalizations and political spin required to continue arming a country committing war crimes.

I worked closely with Sullivan, Blinken, and McGurk through the Obama years and have collaborated with them on projects outside government. Each holds Ivy League degrees and took different paths to advance rapidly to the top of the national security apparatus. Sullivan was a close confidante and protégé of Hillary Clinton at the State Department and on her presidential campaigns. Blinken was Joe Biden’s top staffer for years on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and then joined him in the Obama White House. McGurk worked in Iraq during the Bush administration and continued to do so after Obama’s election.

What they (and I) share is the experience of operating within the machinery of America’s post–September 11 foreign policy. For twenty-five years the US has been at war, normalizing the killing of people from North Africa to South Asia. The powers of the presidency have mushroomed relative to those of Congress, while support for Israel has become more vigorously policed within our politics. All these factors converged in the Biden administration’s post–October 7 policies.

On multiple occasions Blinken invoked emergency measures to rush arms to Israel, bypassing standard protocols that required prenotification to Congress. When Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen pressed the administration to adhere to prohibitions on arming a military committing war crimes, Sullivan proposed a compromise. The result was National Security Memorandum 20, an executive action that required the State Department to investigate whether governments receiving military aid were committing human rights abuses or impeding US humanitarian aid, and the president to “remediate the situation” by suspending weapons transfers. This unleashed a monthslong process to determine whether Israel was, in fact, violating international law. Unusual decisions were made. For instance, Deborah Lipstadt, an envoy for combating antisemitism, was involved in those determinations even though she had no experience adjudicating violations of the laws of war.

Reading about these endless meetings, I remembered that participants must leave smartphones outside White House and State Department rooms. Picture those officials sitting in windowless rooms without their phones, incapable of reaching a formal conclusion that a single war crime was committed in Gaza while the world watched war crimes live-streamed on theirs. Kafka himself might have had a hard time conjuring such a bureaucracy.

Ahmed provides a particularly effective account of the administration’s failure to dislodge Israel’s systematic restrictions on food, medicine, and other aid. Sullivan and McGurk, in his account, became fixated on persuading Netanyahu to allow a trickle of aid trucks into Gaza but did not leverage US military assistance to force a more fundamental change in Israel’s policy of starving the enclave. Airdrops were launched despite warnings that they were an inefficient, dehumanizing, and dangerous way to deliver aid. (Some Palestinians were killed and wounded by the drops.) Biden ordered the US military to build a $230 million pier off the coast of Gaza to deliver assistance that should have been driven across the border in trucks—a plan that failed spectacularly (the pier fell apart) but that had Netanyahu’s support.

One exception to this contorted approach took place after an Israeli strike killed seven staffers of José Andrés’s World Central Kitchen. While Israel had previously killed aid workers in Gaza, this strike drew outsize attention in Washington, where Andrés is a beloved local restaurateur and humanitarian. Biden responded with unusual public outrage, and Israel allowed a large (albeit temporary) spike in aid trucks crossing the border. It was a fleeting success that belied the president’s theory that public pressure on Israel did not work—a lesson the administration chose to ignore.

At the center of Ahmed’s account is that “red line” Biden drew over the Israeli invasion of Rafah in the spring of 2024. Despite pledges to moderate its operations in response to Biden’s pressure, when Israel launched its offensive, a UN worker tells Ahmed, “we lost access to everything overnight,” escalating the aid crisis. Despite Biden’s warnings, Israel killed, wounded, and displaced Palestinians in enormous numbers. An unnamed White House official calls Rafah “one of the most upsetting moments” of a two-decade career in foreign policy.

In response, a single shipment of two-thousand-pound US bombs was paused. This was hardly a cutoff, and yet still Netanyahu attacked Biden for endangering Israel’s security. The administration furiously countered by citing all the support that it was providing to Netanyahu. Biden and his team had started a fight that they didn’t want to win. The weapons kept flowing. Any prospect of exerting meaningful leverage was over.

From that point on Biden and his team retreated deeper into a defensive crouch, backing an Israeli government that was plainly ignoring them. In May 2024 Biden delivered a speech announcing that Israel had accepted the framework of a cease-fire even as Netanyahu was publicly saying the opposite. No matter: for months administration spokespeople cast Hamas as the impediment to an agreement while the Israeli campaign continued unabated.

Ahmed portrays a Democratic administration falling out of step with a growing number of its voters. Biden’s communications team accused reporters who challenged their approach, like Ahmed, of aiding Hamas. Instead, he writes, they focused on cable television, Washington think tanks, and friendly outlets like The Atlantic. When Congress passed, and Biden signed, a long-stagnant bill banning TikTok, lawmakers cited the platform’s perceived bias against Israel as one of the reasons why.

Ahmed also describes officials trapped in their own feedback loops as encampments sprang up across American campuses protesting US support for the war on Gaza. An aide told Ahmed that one senior National Security Council staffer, influenced by cable news coverage, “had no clue about the protesters’ demands but called them ‘pro-Hamas.’” The administration used its bully pulpit to condemn antisemitism in ways that did little to recognize what was motivating most protesters. “This blatant anti-Semitism is reprehensible and dangerous,” Biden declared, “and it has absolutely no place on college campuses.” Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University protest leader and green card holder who was detained for 104 days under Trump despite committing no crime, told Ahmed that “the Biden administration laid the groundwork to my detention.”

As the 2024 election approached, Biden officials were simultaneously running the most powerful government in the world and, in Ahmed’s account, behaving as if they were powerless to change their own policies. No Palestinian was permitted to speak at the Democratic National Convention despite the efforts of members of the Uncommitted National Movement who had opposed Biden’s Gaza policy and renomination but were looking for ways to motivate its supporters to back Kamala Harris. The weapons kept flowing even as officials voiced frustration with Netanyahu in anonymous comments to reporters. Israel escalated its war in Lebanon even as negotiations intended to avoid that escalation were ongoing.

After the election the Biden administration aggressively lobbied Democrats to vote against a Bernie Sanders–backed bill to block weapons transfers to Israel. Ahmed obtained White House talking points sent to Congress that equated casting a vote for the legislation with helping Hamas and Hezbollah, echoing the Israeli prime minister, who was gleefully welcoming Trump’s return. “The lame-duck administration,” Ahmed writes, “was at most a mix of arsenal and punching bag.”

To enter the rooms where these policies are debated and decided, you first pass through gates protected by armed Secret Service agents. You receive an intelligence briefing that uses euphemisms like “noncombatants” to describe the killing of children. You are handed memos teeing up a decision to transfer weapons to the Israeli government that look identical to countless other memos that fill your inbox.

You sit in a meeting in which dissent on that memo is not welcome and the outcome feels preordained. You have discussions about plans to get more aid into Gaza and convince yourself that you’re trying to save the lives those weapons are taking. Maybe you start thinking about the next meeting on a less punishing subject, or head to the carryout window of the White House mess to get a sandwich. Or maybe you convince yourself that your support for Netanyahu is a necessary evil to defeat Donald Trump and save democracy.

The people you hear from directly are likely to reinforce what you’re doing: the big donors who congratulate you after some statement of support for Israel; the members of Congress who tell you to hang in there; the cable news talking heads, think tankers, and opinion writers. You don’t talk to Palestinians or Lebanese. You don’t speak to aid workers on the ground in Gaza. You don’t even spend much time scrolling through Instagram or TikTok (and if you do, your algorithm is probably not feeding you the content enraging so many people outside your silo).

There is something banal about how the days blend together: meetings, memos, phone calls, meals eaten exhaustedly at your desk. Yet as automatic as it all feels, you are participating in life-and-death decisions; you are making choices, even if they feel inevitable.

Ahmed highlights the few Biden officials who chose to resign and speak out. Josh Paul—a former State Department official responsible for arms transfers who quit shortly after October 7—publicly opposed one of those arms packages that was expedited outside normal procedures. He dissented in what Ahmed describes as “a blistering LinkedIn post.”

At first I read that as an unintentionally tragicomic description of the asymmetry of power: while his former colleagues ran the US government, Paul was writing LinkedIn posts. Yet perhaps that misreads the nature of power itself. Because if all you do in government is operate imperial machinery to a predetermined end, what power do you really have? Sure, someone like Paul could not directly influence outcomes once he left government. But he was acting on his own belief about what is right and what is wrong, and there’s a different kind of power in that.

Paul was hardly alone. While those officials were sitting in windowless rooms, much of the world was increasingly distraught over the United States and Israel’s conduct, even as many storied institutions of journalism seemed reluctant to challenge it. Palestinians used social media to show what was happening in Gaza, and in turn, they started to be seen.

I spoke only a few times to Biden officials during these events—usually to complain about their policy or to hear their complaints about something I’d said about it online. I was struck by how much we seemed to inhabit different realities. Mostly I heard arguments about what they felt they could not do: Biden was set in his ways or Netanyahu would ignore their pressure. Or they argued that they were doing more than I saw. Or they speculated that they would pay a higher political price for breaking with Israel than for supporting it. In other words, I heard a version of the story Ahmed tells.

I left those conversations feeling anger and frustration but also a measure of concern for the well-being of the people saying these things. Not because I excused what the Biden team was doing, but because of what they were doing to themselves.

I lived the hypocrisy of American foreign policy for eight years. I was proud of many things: the Iran nuclear deal, the Paris Climate Agreement, and the normalization of relations with Cuba, which I negotiated. I was also deeply conflicted about the violence that I had to defend: the surge in Afghanistan, drone strikes, sanctions that took lives. At the time I told myself that the good outweighed the bad. Since then, I’ve had to reckon with doubts about whether that’s true, or—even if it was—why it was so normal for me to tolerate that equation. But in all my years in the White House, I never had to support something that a UN inquiry found to be genocide.

Make no mistake: Biden and his team are responsible for a Gaza policy that was extreme even by the standards of US foreign policy, a policy that reinforced the global perception that Americans refuse to reckon with the violence the US systematically unleashes on the world while its officials talk about democratic values and a rules-based order. Throughout the war on Gaza, the Biden administration continued to speak about American exceptionalism. We like to think that “exceptionalism” describes a virtuous nation with an indispensable global responsibility. But for much of the world, it describes a superpower exempting itself and Israel from the rules that it demands others follow. The Biden administration strenuously objected to the credible findings that a “genocide” took place under their watch but did not hesitate to describe what China did to Uyghurs or what ISIS did to Yazidis as genocides.

Ultimately, we are defined both by the choices we make and by the choices we don’t make, not by the versions of ourselves that live in our heads. The aide who told Ahmed that the killing in Rafah “slowed and it was not just because there was nobody left to kill” probably believed what he was saying. That is how you rationalize participation in a system that should be untenable.

Crossing the Red Line appears at a time when public opinion has shifted dramatically on Israel and Palestine. But as we approach another presidential campaign, it is not clear whether the Democratic Party or its national security establishment has reckoned with Gaza. Its leadership in Congress—Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries—still welcomes AIPAC’s support and votes to arm the Israeli government.

Biden’s senior officials have expressed some regrets over their Gaza policy but have not stated clearly and categorically that what they did was wrong. McGurk has recently released a book that focuses on the administration’s effort to secure the release of Israeli hostages without confronting its complicity in the violence rained down on Palestinians.* Instead, he describes the rare instances of Biden putting public pressure on Israel as counterproductive.

The extremism of Donald Trump makes it easier for Democrats to avoid self-reproach. An oft-repeated Joe Biden maxim was “Don’t compare me to the Almighty, compare me to the alternative.” Everyone benefits from a comparison with Trump. But Biden’s disregard for international law in Gaza and his demonization of those who protested his Gaza policy foreshadowed the Trump administration’s dismantling of the international order and its attacks on dissent, higher education, and free speech. Meanwhile the growing disconnect between US policy and public opinion on Israel contributes to a sense that perhaps politics don’t matter at all: How can politicians and senior officials be trusted to fight for anything we care about, whether ending wars or lowering prices, if people in power can get away with insisting that what we see happening is not happening?

All of this requires a deeper reckoning by the Democratic Party than has taken place to date. Near the end of his book, Ahmed sums up the mindset that must change:

The implication from Biden’s circle—a big part of the Democratic brain trust that hopes to regain positions of power in post-Trump politics—has consistently been that the greater offense is not in the horror of the war but in questioning those who shaped it.

But those who fail to reckon with the horror that took place in Gaza cannot be trusted to act differently in the future. We do not have to accept that what we are seeing in Gaza and the West Bank is inevitable any more than we have to accept that our grim American present is permanent.

Of course, there are many Americans who care deeply about Israel. As someone who comes from a Jewish background, with family members who perished in the Holocaust, I understand that a commitment to the safety of Jews as a people is connected to the depth of feeling that many have for Israel. But Jewish safety—in Israel or the US—is not served by insisting that the might of a superpower should be enlisted to help Israel carry out the atrocities we have witnessed. The policy of no daylight has been damaging to both America and Israel. It must end, and the mindset of people in future Democratic administrations must be different.

Something is shifting in our culture. The fever of self-censorship is breaking. The cost of complicity is rising. The plight of Palestinians is at last being seen. An awareness is building that there is an alternative: a moral awakening out of the ashes of moral abomination.

“For any event, there is an infinite number of possible outcomes. Our choices determine which outcomes will follow. But there is a theory in quantum physics that all possibilities that can happen or could happen do happen in alternate quantum realities.” This summary of the many-worlds interpretation of quantum physics, a theory first proposed by the American physicist Hugh Everett in the 1950s, is given by a sentient android named Data serving as an officer on the Federation starship USS Enterprise. Technically it’s delivered by the actor Brent Spiner, performing as Data, at a pivotal moment in “Parallels,” an episode from the seventh and final season of Star Trek: The Next Generation. In that episode Data’s fellow officer Worf, a Klingon, returns to the Enterprise after some time spent at an intergalactic sports competition, only to discover that he has passed through a hole in space-time—there’s always a hole in space-time—and that the reality he now inhabits is different from the one he left, in ways that are subtle and profound, comic and tragic.

Most strictly scientific formulations of the many-worlds interpretation hold that there is no practical way to move between branching quantum realities, or even to prove that these alternate realities exist, except as far-out mathematical possibilities. For Star Trek, getting Worf back to his home reality is as simple as flying back through that pesky space-time fissure, then sealing it with a blast from the ship’s engines.

While the theory has been the subject of intense debate within the scientific community—Stephen Hawking and Richard Feynman believed it to be likely true; the Nobel Prize–winning Dutch physicist Gerard ’t Hooft has rejected it as implausible—popular culture has run away with the idea of a multiverse in which every possible iteration of reality can coexist. In recent years, superhero movie franchises have become jittery, reality-hopping narratives of rebooting, recycling, and reincarnation, grafting the idea of infinitely branching realities onto old-fashioned tales of good guys punching bad guys. Setting your stories within a multiverse creates the opportunity for endless marketable derivatives: if a beloved character is killed in one film, you simply open up an inter-universal portal and let them stroll back in during the next.

On a less mercenary, more personal level, exploring alternate realities is a deeply human urge. Most of us, especially in moments of stress or depression, picture other careers, other partners, other selves, often looking for the decisions that allowed our current circumstances to come into being. We don’t always do this in a posture of regret: sometimes we want to confirm the thesis that the life we are currently living is, in fact, the best of all possible lives. Or, at least, not one of the worst.

How It Works Out, a raunchy, hilarious, and occasionally unsettling debut novel in stories by the Canadian writer Myriam Lacroix, is filled with exactly these kinds of speculation. The book is a literary cabinet of curiosities, from which spill alternate realities in ways that are as thunderingly literal and self-consciously silly as any episode of Star Trek but that are also clever, surprising, and deeply felt.

Lacroix grew up in Montreal and now lives in Vancouver with her partner, Allison. That kind of personal detail may seem irrelevant in a book review, but it’s important for understanding Lacroix’s debut, in which the stories are linked by the names of their main characters: Myriam and Allison, who are presented as different people in each tale but who often share biographical facts with the writer and her real-life partner. (How much any of these fictional Myriams and Allisons resemble the actual ones we can only guess and, in the case of the book’s darker stories, hope that the answer is “not much.”)

To describe what happens in How It Works Out is to risk getting lost in an appellative tangle. For example, there is the real-life Myriam Lacroix, the one who is the author of the book, and then there is the Myriam Lacroix of “The Sequel,” the book’s fifth story. That Myriam is a mentally troubled former barista who achieved enormous cultural, critical, and financial success with a book called How It Works Out: Building a Healthy Lesbian Relationship in the Patriarchy, which she cowrote with her partner, Allison. This fictional version of How It Works Out is uncompromisingly political. “Even lesbians who succeed at marriage ultimately fail,” the book asserts, “for they have succeeded only in infiltrating an institution that hates them.”

The book was a best seller, we learn, with copies “on every queer woman’s shelf.” But now, a decade after its publication, sales have evaporated. The culture has shifted; those queer women’s bookshelves have been cleared to make room for even more uncompromising manifestos. “The new generation doesn’t find us radical enough,” Allison, the story’s narrator, tells us. “Nobody cares if a couple of Canadian lesbians have a happy ending.” Their agent, Steve, however, has a plan that involves the kind of rebranding attempted by many C-list celebrities in the era of Trump. Allison sums it up:

Advertisement

If we can’t win over the queer feminists, we might have a chance with the right-wing lesbians, the gated-community dykes. They’re the ones with disposable income, anyway. First step was to get married, get the media’s attention, show publishers the names Myriam and Allison still mean something.

At the moment when Allison says “I do” in a lavish ceremony at a luxe hotel in the mountains, she has trouble staying focused, given all that is happening to make the event go viral: “I’m distracted by the Elle Canada photographer, whose finger is going at the shutter button like she’s trying to get it off. Steve is typing like crazy on his phone, live-tweeting.” Allison is the more fame-skeptical and emotionally grounded of the pair, but she’s not above a bit of clickbaiting of her own: when she kisses her new bride, she slips in “some tongue for the press,” then takes care to smile in a way that shows off her “crooked canine, which some internet forums agree is my best attribute.”

Steve’s rebranding strategy appears, at first, to go well: the actor Kristen Stewart retweets one of the wedding photos; #MAwedding and #howitworksout start trending. But then Myriam, who suffers from extreme fits of paranoia and fear, becomes ill after eating a salad, and Allison begins an intense affair with the doctor who treats her. The story then jumps ahead in time, positing a future in which Myriam is out of the picture and Allison has achieved fame with her second wife, the doctor, with whom she has had a baby. The story ends with the happy couple dancing on set with Ellen DeGeneres before a live studio audience, as confetti falls from the ceiling.

The satire in “The Sequel” is as dark as it is meta. (And it is very meta: the real-life Canadian lesbian sister pop duo Tegan and Sara, who blurbed the actual Lacroix’s actual book, make a cameo in the story as the kind of bored, cynical celebrities who get paid to hang out at weddings.) The gags are so sharp, it’s possible to miss the more thoughtful story happening behind them. Lacroix (the real-life one) wants to do more than merely skewer the most obvious excesses of 2024-era clout chasing. The Allison character, though she is a willing partner in the rebranding, mostly goes along with it because she is fighting to stay close to Myriam, whose illnesses and obsessions threaten to dissolve all the joy left in their relationship. Remove the cultural fame, the agent, and the celebrity wedding, and she is any partner attempting Hail Mary passes to find their way back to what they had before, to fly the spaceship back through the hole in space-time.

Given that Lacroix is a relative unknown in the literary world, the sheer audacity of building her first book from funhouse-mirror distortions of her own life is impressive. Imagine Nicolas Cage playing up his own outsize persona in a film like The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent (2022) before having starred in anything else. How It Works Out could have easily turned out a pointless, self-indulgent mess. But Lacroix presents her outrageous scenarios as settled facts, without any special pleading or giving the reader an opportunity for doubt. The opening of the book’s first story, “The Meaning of Life,” contains all these strengths in compressed form:

They’d planned on getting beer from Toby’s, but instead they got a baby, and they were not unhappy about it. Myriam and Allison hadn’t talked about kids yet, but finding one seemed to be a sign that it was time. Besides, being lesbians, this spared them the trouble of adopting or getting one of their friends to have sex with them.

Here, as she does throughout the book, Lacroix writes with a mixture of emotional coolness and disarming jokiness. The tossed-off gags seem to signal, “Hey, everything’s OK here, reader,” when it quickly becomes apparent that everything is not: the comic shrug in that last line allows us to accept the freakish behavior that follows without the sense of judgment that might be prompted by a more dour literary reality.

In this version of the Myriam–Allison relationship, the pair are the kind of hip, young urbanites who spot an old couch and immediately wonder “if they could turn it into some sort of art installation.” They are also the kind of people who, having found a baby in an alleyway, decide to take it home and name it Jonah, because “they had no idea what Jonahs were like, and they liked the element of surprise.” Taking care of a baby challenges and deepens their understanding of the world. “Nuclear families were a concept made up by the same people who wanted you to get full-time jobs or sell your art for money,” Myriam thinks. “Still, when she lifted Jonah from Allison’s heaving chest and held him in her arms, she could feel the exact dimensions of her happiness, its weight and humid breath. It wasn’t a dream.”

Advertisement

It turns out that Baby Jonah belongs to Dina, an unhappy woman who lost track of her kid while her husband, Ken, was getting beaten up for obnoxiously heckling a comedian. The loss of her child causes the already miserable Dina to crash emotionally, but also brings her newfound clarity: “Realizing that she felt like shit was a bit better than feeling like shit but being too dissociated to realize it. Now, if she started to punch her steering wheel, she knew why she was punching it.”

The Myriam–Allison and Dina–Ken pairings in the story are stereotypes, if not quite caricatures. (Ken, true to clichéd form, is a foulmouthed and lazy brute who sits on his basement-apartment couch spouting homophobic curses while watching hockey; the presence of a stained undershirt is not explicitly mentioned, but it can be inferred.) This flattening of character is intentional: the story, despite its moments of violence, plays out like a fable, with Dina deciding to leave Ken and join the girls in raising Jonah. These people inhabit a gauzy fantasy world, which belies the fact that the story is about a young couple kidnapping an abandoned baby.

The soft focus of that first story works as a setup for the nightmare of the next, “Love Bun,” in which Myriam is a depressed postgraduate being supported by Allison as she struggles to complete a “thesis on trauma, and the cycle of abuse, in the works of certain realist writers.” After a cooking accident, Myriam discovers that eating a small slice of Allison’s flesh makes her feel “giddy and light, like I’d been pumped full of helium.” It also sharpens other appetites: “Three orgasms later, I ate an entire bowl of penne primavera.”

Shortly after that incident, Allison loses a finger in an ice-skating mishap, and Myriam does the unthinkable: she keeps the finger and eats it raw. (It has a “tangy umami flavor.”) The effect is immediate:

It felt like emerging from some sort of primordial glue. I could smell the flowers under the snow, waiting to be born. An elderly woman smiled and I could see behind her teeth, into her throat, down her esophagus, right inside the pouch of her stomach, where love was brewing like a dark green potion. Love was everywhere. Rows of shops sprung out of the sidewalk like pages from a pop-up book, bricks so bright with their own light I could hardly look.

It gets worse. Myriam and Allison decide to have children, whom, with a grim sense of inevitability, they eat—only taking tiny nibbles of some of them, consuming others whole. The cannibalistic descriptions in the story are vivid, difficult to read, and visceral (literally so). It is here that Lacroix’s approach most resembles the horror-infused literary parables often associated with writers like Carmen Maria Machado (Her Body and Other Parties), Kristen Roupenian (Cat Person and Other Stories), and Rachel Yoder (Nightbitch). Lacroix does not spare the violence or the blood, but even as the horrors of “Love Bun” are compounding, she keeps the jokes coming: the depraved couple name their children things like Framboise and Kale. When their firstborn, Jonah—Lacroix’s book is lousy with callbacks—gets a life sentence for eating a male friend, Allison blames the verdict on homophobia. (These stories, incidentally, serve as an excellent corrective to the claims that “wokeism” has taken all the edge out of comedy: How It Works Out is uncompromising and exact in its targeting of people on all sides of various culture wars, and yet manages never to punch down.)

“Love Bun” represents the most extreme and horrifying variation on Myriam–Allison. (The oddest is “Mantis,” in which Allison is a pet dog, Myriam a pet mantis in a terrarium.) The levels of surrealism change from story to story, though in almost all of them reality feels both heightened and warped. The interpersonal dynamics shift, too: sometimes Myriam is the villain, sometimes it’s Allison, sometimes both. The one constant is that at least one of the partners yearns for the other. Even in its strangest scenarios, the Myriams and Allisons of How It Works Out exhibit the most basic of needs, the need for love.

The answers to whether any of these variants actually fulfill this need range from “of course” to “of course not,” but even in the book’s darkest moments, there is no doubt that love is worth struggling for. This romantic core, though often buried under much cultural and personal rubble, is what distinguishes Lacroix’s book from the more pessimistic visions of Roupenian et al. These are dark stories, but they have an undeniably sentimental heart, which keeps them from feeling like too clever experiments. Even when the Myriams and Allisons are presented as monsters, we somehow want them to be together, and feel genuine sadness when they can’t manage it. As for the fate of the actual Myriam and Allison, that is somewhat spoiled by the book’s dedication page: “To Allison, I figured it out. I know how it works out.”

entries.title: One Battle After Another
entries.summary: Two new histories of the Red Brigades explain how terrorism took hold in the wealthiest parts of Italy in the 1970s.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Shortly after I moved to Italy in early January 1980, someone assassinated the governor of Sicily. It was eventually found to be a Mafia killing, but at the time everyone I met wondered whether the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades), the country’s main left-wing terrorist group, had begun operating in Sicily. The next day I went to visit a friend of my father’s, an old journalist recovering from throat cancer. While we sat talking, there was a knock at the door, followed by several seconds of panicked silence, since the journalist’s name had turned up on a Red Brigades list of potential targets. It turned out to be a young woman to whom my hosts had wanted to introduce me. The journalist’s wife asked if she had been in Lotta Continua (Continuous Struggle) in high school, referring to a far-left group that had been especially active in the early 1970s.

For young Italians of our visitor’s generation, adherence to one of a number of radical student groups had been an almost obligatory rite of passage, like belonging to a college fraternity in the United States. Two days after the governor of Sicily was murdered, the Red Brigades killed three police agents in the center of Milan, where I was living. The head of the publishing house where I worked had a bodyguard and a bulletproof car. Police armed with submachine guns combed the subways, checking people’s documents. I met a young man whose mother had been kidnapped and others whose older siblings had not been seen in a few years; it was feared that they had disappeared into the underground world of armed struggle.

In Milan at that time, it was obvious that, despite all the political violence, Italy was becoming an extremely wealthy society. The cities and towns of central and northern Italy, where terrorist groups thrived, had a standard of living the rest of the world could envy. I remember visiting Bergamo, a prosperous medium-sized industrial city, and seeing the symbol of the Red Brigades painted on a wall; it was a Sunday, the streets were deserted, and you could hear the clatter of plates and forks as the bergamaschi sat down to what were no doubt delicious meals. How had terrorism taken hold in the wealthiest parts of a country with one of the world’s fastest-growing economies? John Foot’s The Red Brigades and Sergio Luzzatto’s Dolore e furore offer explanations as well as gripping narratives of Italian terrorism.

Foot, a professor of modern Italian history at the University of Bristol, begins The Red Brigades with brief sketches of the group’s founding members. Renato Curcio was born into a working-class family in 1941, the illegitimate son of a single mother. One of his uncles, a partisan during the war, was killed by the fascists; when Curcio needed a code name in his clandestine life in the Red Brigades he chose Armando, his uncle’s first name. In his twenties he enrolled in the University of Trento’s sociology department, which became something of an incubator of left-wing radicals. Like many Italian universities, Trento was caught up in the fervor of the 1960s student movement fueled by Vietnam War protest and the popularity of China’s Cultural Revolution. “By 1967 Curcio was calling himself a Marxist and a Maoist,” Foot writes. That year

he co-authored one of the most influential documents to emerge from the student movement—a Manifesto for a Negative University. This manifesto went beyond a radical critique of university to a rejection of society in general. It argued that “repression and violence are the connective tissue” of Italian democracy.

The following year students occupied the university for sixty-seven days.

Curcio fell in love with a fellow Trento sociology student, Margherita (Mara) Cagol, who like him came from a devout Catholic family. The young couple fused the tradition of Catholic social activism with a form of radical Marxism; they were driven by a moral imperative to fight for the oppressed and bring about a Communist revolution. Curcio and Cagol married and moved in 1969 from provincial Trento to Milan, which was one of the centers of Italian industry. There they became close friends with Alberto Franceschini, who became the third founding member of the Red Brigades.

Franceschini was part of a militant strain within the Italian Communist Party (Partito Comunista Italiano, or PCI). He came from the city of Reggio Emilia—part of Italy’s Red Belt. His grandfather had been a founding member of the party, and the area was a stronghold of partisan resistance to fascism during and after World War II. As Communist partisans had formed the largest and strongest resistance groups, many of them expected that their struggle would lead to armed revolution. Instead the leadership of the PCI embraced Italian democracy: the party governed scores of cities across the center-north and focused on improving social services such as childcare, schools, transportation, and support for the elderly. The PCI was evolving into a reformist social democratic force, but it still paid lip service to the idea of Communist revolution.

Advertisement

Franceschini’s dissident group in Emilia-Romagna included former partisans who kept their old guns oiled for when they might be needed. In Foot’s formulation, Italian terrorism was something of a three-legged stool, combining the student radicalism of 1968, the increasingly militant mood in Italy’s factories, and the frustrated revolutionary elements of the Italian left who felt that the antifascist resistance had been betrayed. These three traditions came together when Curcio, Cagol, and Franceschini began working with the radicals in the Milan factories and became active members of a new organization, the Comitato Unitario di Base (Unitary Base Committee), which brought together workers, students, militants, and local residents and operated outside the official unions at the Pirelli tire factory.

“These activities were noisy, boisterous, occasionally joyful, undisciplined, angry and often violent,” Foot writes.

Workers brought production lines to a halt without warning and were difficult to control. Demonstrations on the factory floor, heralded by the banging of drums, whistles and the smashing of metal on metal, would arrive from nowhere and shut down work. Those who disobeyed would often be threatened, or chased away, or forced to join in, sometimes with ropes which literally pulled people in.

Strikes spread across northern Italy in what became known as the Hot Autumn of 1969, with more radical groups that identified with the Viet Cong promising to turn the country’s factories into “one, two, three Vietnams.”

The combination of student protest and worker militancy was proving incendiary. In this overheated situation, someone planted a bomb in the lobby of a bank in Milan’s Piazza Fontana on December 12, 1969, killing seventeen people and injuring nearly ninety. Police began a roundup of hundreds of left-wing militants and arrested an anarchist railroad worker, Giuseppe Pinelli. Three days after the bombing, Pinelli fell or was pushed out the window of the room where he was being interrogated. The authorities insisted that he had committed suicide after confessing his guilt.

Eventually the militants were found to be innocent, and evidence pointed toward a neofascist group based in Padua that may have had murky ties with members of the Italian secret service. The Piazza Fontana bombing was the most glaring example of what came to be known as “the strategy of tension,” in which elements of the far right committed acts meant to create an atmosphere of chaos and violence that would push the country in an authoritarian direction or even provoke a military coup. It was the point at which many Italians claimed to have “lost their innocence.”

Weeks after the bombing, the book publisher Giangiacomo Feltrinelli wrote an open letter announcing that he was leaving the country. “He claimed,” Foot writes,

that the bomb in Piazza Fontana signalled “the end of democratic illusions,” complained about judicial investigations against him, and said that Piazza Fontana was Italy’s “little Reichstag,” a reference to the events that facilitated the intensification of Nazism in Germany and its crackdown on freedoms and rights.

Feltrinelli—the heir to one of the largest fortunes in Italy—was a friend and admirer of Fidel Castro and considered himself a fighter against imperialism. Along with serious works of literature, he had published scores of revolutionary pamphlets, books by Che Guevara, books exalting the Tupamaros—the Uruguayan urban terrorist group—and even a practical manual for urban guerrillas by the Brazilian revolutionary Carlos Marighella, which became one of the bibles of groups like the Red Brigades. Rather than leave Italy, Feltrinelli went underground, began going by the code name Osvaldo, and tried to organize armed revolution.

In 1970 Curcio, Cagol, and Franceschini formed the Red Brigades. Their symbol—a five-pointed yellow star inside a red circle—was modeled on that of the Tupamaros. From the beginning, what distinguished the Red Brigades from the dozens of other groups in what was called the “extraparliamentary left” was their single-minded focus on political violence. Other groups (such as Lotta Continua and Potere Operaio) had small armed contingents and preached revolution, but their leaders remained public figures, holding conventions, publishing newspapers, and in some cases participating in elections. They were divided over the place of violence in the revolution. In March 1972 Feltrinelli blew himself up while trying to place a bomb on a pylon outside Milan in order to sabotage the city’s electrical grid. Two months later what were likely militants of Lotta Continua assassinated Luigi Calabresi, the police commissioner who had interrogated Giuseppe Pinelli. Disagreements over violence (among other things) eventually led to the group’s breakup in 1976. In 1973 members of Potere Operaio firebombed the apartment of a neofascist, accidentally killing his two sons, aged twenty-two and eight. The crime horrified many in the group and contributed to its dissolution later that year.

Advertisement

The Red Brigades were much more professional, disciplined, and rigorous in following Marighella’s manual of urban warfare. They bought guns and trained themselves to use them. When members went underground, they cut all ties with friends and family and assumed new identities. These full-time “regular members,” who carried out military operations, were flanked by a larger number of irregular members who provided various kinds of logistical support: renting hideout apartments, supplying legal and medical help, and gathering information to assist with the activities of the regular members. Following the Leninist model of Communist cells, contact between members was kept to the minimum necessary so that if any were arrested, their knowledge of the group was limited.

The Red Brigades’ early success was partly the result of the state’s lack of preparation. Italy was then trying to reform and liberalize aspects of its judicial system. It had no laws to deal adequately with this new kind of threat. If a Red Brigades member was arrested on suspicion of participating in a crime, he would be released awaiting trial and then disappear underground. In 1974 Curcio was arrested and a year later was brought to a small prison in Casale Monferrato in Piedmont. Cagol and another comrade turned up on visiting day, forced their way into the prison with guns, and freed him. This made Cagol and Curcio into outlaw folk heroes, the Bonnie and Clyde of the revolutionary left. When Cagol was killed four months later during a police raid, she became a martyr to the cause.

Both The Red Brigades and Dolore e furore cover the events that helped shape Italy’s so-called Years of Lead: from the Piazza Fontana bombing in 1969, the death of Feltrinelli, the Calabresi killing, and the gradual escalation of violence to the group’s demise in the early-to-mid-1980s. The Red Brigades’ initial actions focused on factory life: burning the cars of unpopular managers or taking them prisoner for brief periods. In these early kidnappings, they generally did not harm their victims; instead they interrogated them and put them on trial, symbolically substituting proletarian justice for the repression of the state. From there they moved to kneecapping or shooting their victims in the legs and then to longer-term kidnappings and assassinations. As the Italian state began to react more vigorously, the Red Brigades retaliated by killing police officers and kidnapping or killing judges.

These attacks on the “heart of the state” culminated in the spectacular kidnapping of five-time prime minister Aldo Moro, the president of the ruling Christian Democratic Party (Democrazia Cristiana, or DC). Moro was the primary architect of the “historic compromise,” a rapprochement between the conservative DC and the PCI. The PCI at this point enjoyed the support of about 34 percent of the Italian electorate and was close to overtaking the DC’s 38 percent, but its leader, Enrico Berlinguer, felt that it would be dangerous to form a government without a solid majority. In Chile the socialist leader Salvador Allende had come to power with only a plurality and had been overthrown in a violent right-wing coup in 1973. The solution, Berlinguer and Moro concluded, was cooperation between left and right.

Moro was kidnapped in March 1978 as he was on his way to the Italian Parliament to inaugurate the first government headed by the DC and supported by the PCI. The ambush of his motorcade was carried out flawlessly: all five members of his security detail were killed, and Moro was taken unharmed. The Red Brigades managed to keep him for fifty-five days despite an enormous police manhunt. During that time the entire nation held its breath as his captors issued communiqués and allowed Moro to write numerous letters to family, friends, and fellow politicians in which he begged them to negotiate in order to spare his life.

The terrorists hoped to divide the government and force it into some humiliating compromise that would further damage the credibility of the state and facilitate the cause of revolution, but the leaders of both the DC and the PCI were united in what was called la linea della fermezza (the hard line) against negotiation; it was difficult to make concessions to a group that had murdered the five men guarding Moro. When negotiations failed, the Red Brigades killed Moro and left his body in the trunk of a car parked in the center of Rome—despite all the police roadblocks—roughly equidistant between the headquarters of the DC and the PCI.

These increasingly bold actions made the Red Brigades front-page news but also isolated them from the proletariat in whose name they claimed to be acting. The more professional and militarized they became, the more they had to guard against outside contact and infiltration. The locus of their actions had shifted from the factory to the state. Many of their early victims had associations with the far right, but now they began targeting reformists of the center and the left.

The Red Brigades’ war against the reformist left culminated in the murder in Genoa in 1979 of a Communist unionist, Guido Rossa, who had reported a fellow worker for distributing the group’s leaflets in the factory. In Luzzatto’s view it was the Rossa killing rather than the Moro kidnapping that marked the beginning of the end for the Red Brigades, the moment at which the revolution began devouring its own. The Moro case stunned the Italian public, but the Rossa murder brought hundreds of thousands of ordinary Italians, mostly workers, into the streets to mourn him.

Foot’s book is the best single-volume history in English of the Red Brigades. He makes sound judgments about the relative importance of events, avoids many of the fanciful conspiracy theories that have arisen around the group, and gives a brisk and solid account of its actions. But by focusing on one group in the constellation of the far left in Italy, he inevitably leaves a great deal out. After a while, the book feels like a dutiful chronicle of one Red Brigades battle after another. We never quite get inside the heads of the men and women who were prepared to kill for their cause. Foot relies mainly on the large library of books in Italian on terrorism and the memoirs of former members. He quotes from the group’s many communiqués, which make them sound like ideological fanatics parroting unnuanced Communist propaganda. As a result we don’t fully understand why university professors, medical doctors and lawyers, former antifascist partisans, and factory workers were drawn by the siren call of revolution.

In an afterword, Foot explains why he did not try to interview former brigatisti:

This wasn’t for any moral reason: it was a choice born from reading the many accounts a number of them have produced over the years. In brief, I very much doubted whether they would say anything new to me; I thought that any such meetings would be a waste of time. Perhaps this was a mistake.

I think this was indeed a missed opportunity. In the early 2000s I interviewed several former terrorists and leaders of the revolutionary left, many of whom had been released from prison after serving long sentences. They were almost uniformly smart and interesting people with a complex and nuanced understanding of their experiences and mistakes. “I think it’s probably good we didn’t win, because we had no idea what we would have done,” Franco Piperno, a physics professor and former leader of Potere Operaio, told me.

Luzzatto, an Italian historian at the University of Connecticut, takes a different approach. He focuses on the Red Brigades in one city, his native Genoa, and drills very deep: there doesn’t appear to be an archive he hasn’t scoured; he interviewed dozens of former terrorists as well as their friends and relatives; we learn about the topography of Genoese neighborhoods and the temperature and rainfall on important dates. The book contains scores of portraits of central and peripheral figures, with fascinating asides and digressions, curious scenes, and telling anecdotes and details. At times the level of granular detail can seem overwhelming: the index lists more than a thousand names. But the book manages, quite brilliantly, to be both a microhistory of the Red Brigades and a macrohistory of Italian terrorism.

Perhaps the biggest difference between the two books is that Luzzatto gives a much fuller sense of the fertile soil out of which Italian radicalism grew. He does not discuss the Red Brigades in detail until page 184. In that long prologue, we learn a lot about post–World War II Genoa and some of the archaic institutions and social conditions that caused many of its citizens to rebel: for example, the Nave Scuola Garaventa, a floating reform school docked in the port of Genoa where juvenile delinquents were educated. An antiquated institution that began operation in 1883 and was finally closed in 1977, it was a harsh and punitive place of physical and sexual abuse. A few of its former inmates ended up in the Red Brigades. One of Luzzatto’s main characters, Giovanni Senzani, a professor of criminology, visited the floating reformatory as part of a major study of Italy’s reform schools, and that pushed him toward supporting revolution.

Luzzatto describes the difficult conditions in Genoa’s poorer neighborhoods built into the hills above the city center, which were subject to frequent flooding and landslides. Radical youth groups like Lotta Continua were extremely present in these neighborhoods, offering help and recruiting new members. Luzzatto includes a map of thirty-one different headquarters of various far-left groups operating in Genoa in the 1970s, among them Lotta Continua, Potere Operaio, and Avanguardia Operaia, which served as social centers for young people. They offered classes and services, recruited new members, sold pamphlets and newspapers, were present in high schools and universities, and competed to lead the revolution. It is impossible to understand Italian terrorism without first grasping the activities of these groups, many of whose members later found their way into the ranks of the Red Brigades.

Luzzatto takes us inside the humanities department of the University of Genoa, which also acted as an incubator for local radicalism. One of its most charismatic professors, the historian Gianfranco Faina, briefly teamed up with the Red Brigades and then, perhaps for reasons of personal ego, formed his own (failed) competing armed group, Azione Rivoluzionaria. The department also produced Enrico Fenzi, Senzani’s brother-in-law and a refined scholar of fourteenth-century Italian poetry, who joined the Red Brigades. The weaving together of this dense web of connections begins to make sense of this fraught, heady period. These are people who were reading Michel Foucault’s Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison and who saw the development of Italy’s supposedly generous welfare state as a more subtle form of imprisonment. In the world of the radical left, they were making common cause with working-class people who had experienced the daily violence of factory life and fantasized about beating up their bosses and shitting on their desks. One proletarian brigatista said to Fenzi, “You will never be ferocious. You’ve never been in the factory.”

Riccardo Dura, another of Luzzatto’s main characters, was the child of Sicilian immigrants who moved to northern Italy as part of the migration from the south during Italy’s postwar economic boom. His father disappeared. He had a stormy relationship with his mother, ended up on the reform school ship, served in the army and the merchant marines, then found something of a home in the Genoa chapter of Lotta Continua. He became part of the group of young radicals who sat at the feet of Faina, who then recruited him into the Red Brigades. “Riccardo was somebody who had nothing…. He was the classic case right out of the Marxist doctrine of having nothing to lose but his chains,” one ex-brigatista said of him. “When they asked him: join us and go underground, he suddenly had an apartment, a salary, if small, but more importantly a purpose in life.”

Intellectuals were now joining forces with the disenfranchised people they had been reading and writing about, as if their theories were being proved true and coming to life before their eyes. Someone like Dura had the pent-up anger to do the actual killing that the armed revolution required. Fenzi told Luzzatto:

He was one of those desperate types, not really bad but really angry, with a fire inside….

He inveighed against the shitty Italian people who needed to be treated with a blow torch….

He said to me once: if we ever win, I don’t want honors or a position. One thing: the job of killing all our enemies, all those who need to be taken care of. It will be a big job because millions of people should be eliminated.

Dura appears to have let his anger get the better of him. In the attack on Guido Rossa, the plan was apparently only to shoot him in the legs as punishment for informing on a fellow worker, but Dura ended up killing him instead. Fellow brigatisti considered that a serious mistake, and in Luzzatto’s view it shifted public opinion sharply against the group.

This nihilistic act of proletarian self-destruction was indicative of the blind alley that the Red Brigades were heading into. Their dream of revolution was turning into a purely military battle with the state—a battle they were destined to lose. Dura was killed in a shoot-out with police in 1980. By 1982 virtually all the high-level leaders had been rounded up and sent to prison. Luzzatto correctly describes the Years of Lead as the catastrophe of a generation.

There were already signs, when I lived in Milan in the early 1980s, that the tide of revolution was turning and being replaced by something Italians called il riflusso—“the ebbing of the tide.” Thousands of syringes began to litter Italian parks as a generation of young people shipwrecked by revolution turned to drugs or fled to ashrams in India. In November 1980 the real estate developer Silvio Berlusconi began broadcasts on Italy’s first private national TV network, Canale 5, from offices in the American-style gated community he had created just outside Milan. Showing programs like the American soap opera Dallas, it offered a future entirely different from the revolutionary fervor of the 1960s and 1970s, one of material wealth and pleasure.

The radicalism and extreme politicization of Italy in the 1970s pushed the country toward the right and, perhaps more importantly, toward an increased political apathy. Giovanni Senzani was struck by the change when he emerged after some twenty years of near-total isolation in a maximum-security prison. When I met him in 2000, he explained that he was struck and saddened by how narrow and modest the ambitions of the young Italians of his daughter’s generation were. They had virtually no notion—or hopes—of changing the world. By contrast, his own generation had erred in the opposite direction. “We tried to touch the sky,” he said, and fell to earth.
